title: Lefschetz number of a geometric endomorphism
notes: For \(\cdots\to\Gamma(E_i)\xrightarrow d\Gamma(E_{i+1})\to\cdots\), the maps \(T_i\) commute with \(d\); the notes define \(L(T,E)=\sum_i(-1)^i\operatorname{tr}T_i^*\).
statement: Let \(X\) be a compact smooth manifold without boundary, \((E_\bullet,d)\) a finite elliptic complex, and \(T_i\) continuous endomorphisms of its section spaces satisfying \(d_iT_i=T_{i+1}d_i\). Ellipticity makes \(H^i(E_\bullet)\) finite dimensional. The Lefschetz number is the alternating trace of the induced maps on these cohomology spaces.
reconstruction: Compactness, absence of boundary, finiteness and ellipticity are the analytic setting required by the proof, rather than words repeated at this heading.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Transverse fixed-point formula
notes: The local term is \(\sigma(\rho)=\sum_i(-1)^i\operatorname{Sp}\varphi_i(\rho)/|\det(1-I_f(\rho))|\); the total is a sum over fixed points.
statement: Assume additionally that \(T_i s(x)=\varphi_i(x)s(f(x))\), where \(f:X\to X\) is smooth and \(\varphi_i:f^*E_i\to E_i\) intertwines the complex. If every fixed point \(\rho\) is transverse, equivalently \(\det(I-df_\rho)\ne0\), then \[L(T,E)=\sum_{f(\rho)=\rho}\frac{\sum_i(-1)^i\operatorname{tr}\varphi_i(\rho)}{|\det(I-df_\rho)|}.\] There are finitely many such points on compact \(X\).
reconstruction: The geometric form of \(T\), transversality and the fixed-point index of the outer sum are supplied explicitly. The denominator belongs to the real smooth formula; holomorphic variants package numerator and denominator differently.
fate: Bott's Expos\'e 295 states this formula and dates the lecture to November 1965; its bibliography identifies the Atiyah--Bott Harvard notes of fall 1964. Thus later printing does not make the theorem new in this seminar. \citep{bott1966report}
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Kernel proof and its trace-class obstruction
notes: The notes call the formal proof trivial: \(L=\sum_i(-1)^i\operatorname{tr}T_i\), with kernel \(\varphi\delta(y-f(x))\); its diagonal gives the fixed-point sum.
statement: The finite-dimensional Euler trace identity does not by itself justify traces on infinite-dimensional section spaces. For a transverse geometric endomorphism the distribution kernel restricts to the diagonal and defines a flat trace; its value is the displayed fixed-point sum. Ordinary operator trace need not exist. A smoothing or complex-power argument is required to identify the alternating flat trace with the cohomological trace.
reconstruction: The distinction between ordinary trace and diagonal distributional (flat) trace makes explicit the obstruction acknowledged by the subsequent regularization.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Complex-power regularization and eigenspace cancellation
notes: \(T_{i,z}=(1+\Box_i)^{-z}T_i\), \(\Box=d\delta+\delta d\). A displayed eigenseries lacks a trace on its finite-dimensional summands; the alternating trace is said to continue to all \(z\).
statement: Choose metrics and the formal adjoints \(\delta\). For \(\operatorname{Re}z\) sufficiently large, \((1+\Box_i)^{-z}T_i\) is trace class, with trace \[\sum_\lambda(1+\lambda)^{-z}\operatorname{tr}(\pi_{i,\lambda}T_i\iota_{i,\lambda}).\] The eigenspace complexes at positive \(\lambda\) are acyclic, and their projected endomorphisms have vanishing alternating trace. The remaining harmonic-space trace equals \(L(T,E)\), so the supertrace is constant on its initial domain and extends as that constant.
reconstruction: The finite-dimensional trace in the eigenseries and the projected chain map are explicit repairs. Commutation of \(T\) with \(d\) need not imply commutation with \(\Box\); the projection formulation avoids that unwarranted assumption.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Off-diagonal regularity and the value at zero
notes: The complex-power kernel is smooth away from the diagonal. With separated cutoffs \(\mu_1,\mu_2\), \(\mu_1(1+\Box)^{-z}\mu_2\) has a smooth kernel. At \(z=0\) the continued alternating trace is an integral as a number.
statement: Complex powers of a positive elliptic operator have kernels smooth off the diagonal; localization by smooth cutoffs with disjoint supports is smoothing. Under the fixed-point transversality assumptions the regularized trace has the appropriate holomorphic continuation at zero and there equals the diagonal distributional trace. An unrestricted integral of the unsmoothed kernel is not being asserted.
reconstruction: The unreadable support condition is reconstructed as disjoint supports from both the kernel argument and Bott's regularization. The parenthetical name is identified bibliographically with Kotake--Narasimhan; the scan alone does not settle its letters.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Multiplying distributions conormal to transverse submanifolds
notes: When can distributions singular on transverse submanifolds be multiplied? A sufficient example is \(P\delta_S\), with \(P\) pseudodifferential; the notes prescribe special smooth approximations.
statement: For embedded submanifolds \(S,T\subset X\) meeting transversely and properly supported classical pseudodifferential operators \(P,Q\), the conormal distributions \(P\delta_S\) and \(Q\delta_T\) have a canonical product. Their wavefront sets lie in \(N^*S\setminus0\) and \(N^*T\setminus0\); transversality excludes opposing covectors over a common point. Singular support alone, without a conormal or wavefront restriction, is insufficient to state such a rule.
reconstruction: The wavefront formulation is a modern reconstruction of the sufficient class, not terminology attributed to the notebook. Bott's exposition supplies the transverse-distribution regularization relevant to the fixed-point argument.
fate: The fixed-point flat-trace case is already explicit in Bott's contemporary exposition. The general wavefront multiplication criterion is given and proved by H\"ormander, Theorem 2.5.10, printed pp. 126--127, and yields the conormal sufficient class in the question. Class B records this later precise microlocal development, not a claim that transverse delta multiplication was unknown in 1965. \citep{bott1966report,hormander1971fourier}
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: The transverse delta product
notes: \(\delta(x_1)\delta(x_2)=\delta(x_1,x_2)\), accompanied by crossing lines and a comment that the graph meets the diagonal transversely.
statement: In coordinates \((x_1,x_2,z)\), the product of the integration distributions on \(x_1=0\) and \(x_2=0\) is the distribution \(\phi\mapsto\int\phi(0,0,z)\,dz\), with the chosen coordinate densities. Tensor-product mollifiers give this limit. More generally, a change of transverse defining equations contributes the usual Jacobian determinant.

title: Principal affine opens and localization
notes: \(X_P=\{P\ne0\}\) forms a Zariski basis, with sections \(Q/P^n\). The notes say that \(X_P\) is again an affine space.
statement: If \(X=\operatorname{Spec}A\) is an affine variety over a field and \(P\in A\), then \(D(P)=\operatorname{Spec}A_P\), and \(\Gamma(D(P),\mathcal O_X)=A_P\). It is affine, realized by \(Pt=1\) in \(X\times\mathbb A^1\), but need not be an affine space. For example \(D(x)\subset\mathbb A^1\) is \(\mathbb G_m\).
reconstruction: Here and below \(A\) is the coordinate ring of \(X\), a quotient of a polynomial ring in general.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Finite type and coherent algebraic sheaves
notes: An algebraic sheaf is an \(\mathcal O_X\)-module. Finite type means locally a quotient of a finite direct sum; coherence additionally requires every relation sheaf for a finite set of sections to be of finite type.
statement: An \(\mathcal O_X\)-module \(\mathcal F\) is coherent if it is locally finitely generated and, for every open \(U\) and finite family of local sections, the kernel of the resulting map \(\mathcal O_U^r\to\mathcal F|_U\) is locally finitely generated. Finite generation alone is not the definition on an arbitrary ringed space.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Coherence of structure sheaves by Noetherianity
notes: The relation module of \((Q_1/P^n,\ldots,Q_r/P^n)\) is reduced to a kernel over \(k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), which is finitely generated by Hilbert's theorem.
statement: A finitely generated algebra over a field is Noetherian. Kernels of maps between finite free modules are finitely generated, and localization commutes with their kernels. Consequently \(\mathcal O_X\) is coherent on an affine finite-type variety and, by locality, on every locally Noetherian variety.
reconstruction: For a general affine variety replace the polynomial ring by its defining quotient; the kernel generates the relation sheaf, rather than being a fibre without localization.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Closed subvarieties and quotient sheaves
notes: For closed \(Y\subset X\), the ideal sheaf \(J_Y\) is coherent and \(\mathcal O_X/J_Y=\mathcal O_Y\).
statement: For a closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) of Noetherian varieties, the defining ideal sheaf \(\mathcal I_Y\) and the quotient \(\mathcal O_X/\mathcal I_Y\) are coherent; as sheaves on \(X\), the latter is \(i_*\mathcal O_Y\). The structure sheaf on \(Y\) itself is obtained by restriction to its own ringed space.
reconstruction: The pushforward distinguishes the two underlying spaces suppressed in the notes.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Global generation and acyclicity on an affine variety
notes: First the notes state vanishing for coherent sheaves, and later say that any sheaf is generated by sections and has trivial higher cohomology.
statement: For \(X=\operatorname{Spec}A\), a quasi-coherent sheaf \(\widetilde M\) is generated by its global sections and satisfies \(H^q(X,\widetilde M)=0\) for \(q>0\). On a Noetherian affine variety, coherent sheaves correspond to finite \(A\)-modules. The assertion is not true for arbitrary sheaves.
reconstruction: The coherent or quasi-coherent hypothesis must be restored to the second formulation; it is already present in the preceding line.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Computing cohomology with an affine cover
notes: Affine acyclicity permits calculation with an affine cover; the proof ends with the vanishing of cover cohomology for a principal-open cover \((X_{p_i})\).
statement: For a separated variety and a finite affine cover, finite intersections are affine. The Cech complex of a quasi-coherent sheaf therefore computes its sheaf cohomology. On an affine scheme a finite principal-open cover has an exact augmented Cech complex for a quasi-coherent sheaf.
reconstruction: Separatedness, quasi-coherence and the acyclicity of intersections are the hypotheses used by the Cech-to-derived comparison.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: The unfinished converse to affine acyclicity
notes: The line labelled Chevalley's theorem stops at \(H^i=0\Longrightarrow\), with no consequent.
statement: The natural comparison is Serre's affineness criterion: for a Noetherian scheme, vanishing of \(H^q(X,\mathcal F)\) for every quasi-coherent \(\mathcal F\) and every \(q>0\) characterizes affineness. The notebook does not give the quantifiers or the conclusion; it cannot establish which variant or attribution the speaker intended.
reconstruction: The affineness criterion is offered only as a historically and contextually natural reconstruction, not as a recovered missing phrase.
fate: Serre's affine theory supplies a close comparison, but the unfinished sentence is insufficient for an exact identification of a separate theorem called Chevalley's. \citep{serre1955faisceaux}

title: Hilbert Nullstellensatz and the coordinate ring
notes: If \(P\) vanishes on the variety of an ideal \(J\), then \(P^k\in J\); the notes then identify the ring of sections with \(A=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\).
statement: Over an algebraically closed field \(k\), the strong Nullstellensatz gives \(I(V(J))=\sqrt J\) for \(J\subset k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). If \(X\) is a reduced affine variety, \(\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I(X)\), not the ambient polynomial ring unless \(X=\mathbb A^n\).
reconstruction: The field condition and the quotient implicit in the symbol \(A\) are stated explicitly.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: A section supported on a principal divisor is killed by a power
notes: Lemma 1: if a section \(s\) of a coherent sheaf on affine \(X\) vanishes on \(X_P\), then \(P^m s=0\) for some \(m\).
statement: For \(\mathcal F=\widetilde M\) on \(\operatorname{Spec}A\), a global section \(s\in M\) restricts to zero in \(M_P\) exactly when \(P^m s=0\) for some nonnegative integer \(m\). The localized-module criterion proves the statement, and in fact does not require finite generation of \(M\).

title: The ideal of the origin on the affine line
notes: The notes identify \(k[x]\) with germs of polynomials vanishing at zero and call the quotient one dimensional.
statement: The ideal of global polynomials vanishing at zero is \((x)\subset k[x]\), with \(k[x]/(x)\simeq k\). At the stalk the corresponding ideal is \((x)k[x]_{(x)}\subset k[x]_{(x)}\). The ideal, ambient ring and local ring must be distinguished.

title: Clearing denominators in a coherent subsheaf
notes: Lemma 2: \(\mathcal F\subset\mathcal O_X^n\); a section over \(X_P\) extends to \(X\) after multiplication by a sufficiently high power of \(P\).
statement: Let \(X=\operatorname{Spec}A\) be Noetherian and \(\mathcal F\subset\mathcal O_X^n\) coherent. For \(s\in\Gamma(D(P),\mathcal F)\), first clear its coordinates in \((A_P)^n\), obtaining \(t\in A^n\). The image of \(t\) in \(\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X^n/\mathcal F)\) vanishes after localization and is killed by a further power of \(P\); hence that power times \(t\) lies in \(\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)\).
reconstruction: \ours{} The sentence on P000111 saying that the cleared section may fail to belong to \(\mathcal O_X^n\) must mathematically refer to failure to belong to \(\mathcal F\). The ambient free module already contains the cleared vector.

title: Picard omission and the Nevanlinna defect relation
notes: The notes say that a meromorphic quotient \(a(z)/b(z)\) omits at most two values and that the sum of its defects is at most two.
statement: For a nonconstant meromorphic function \(f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb P^1\), at most two points of \(\mathbb P^1\) are omitted. With the usual characteristic \(T(r,f)\) and counting functions, the Nevanlinna defects satisfy \(\sum_{a\in\mathbb P^1}\delta(a,f)\le2\). The ratio model uses a reduced pair of entire functions, with no common zero; the associated projective curve is the invariant object.
reconstruction: Nonconstancy and the projective interpretation exclude the immediate constant-function counterexample.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Higher-dimensional hyperplane omission requires general position
notes: An entire curve \((a,b,c)\) in three-dimensional space is said to meet every plane through zero except possibly three; a finite number is asserted in dimension \(n\).
statement: For a linearly nondegenerate holomorphic curve \(f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb P^{n-1}\), a collection of omitted hyperplanes in general position has at most \(n\) members. The general-position requirement concerns the collection: any \(n\) defining linear forms are independent. Without nondegeneracy even a constant projective curve avoids infinitely many hyperplanes, so the notebook's unqualified formulation is false.
reconstruction: Linear nondegeneracy and general position are the precise classical hypotheses supplied by the cited value-distribution context; no unrestricted total-hyperplane bound is claimed here.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: The endpoint analytic curve for Sturm--Liouville problems
notes: The equation is \(-y''+p(x)y=\lambda y\) on \([0,\pi]\). One margin has \(y(0)=y'(0)=0\), but the subsequent displayed solution is normalized by \(y(0,\lambda)=0,\ y'(0,\lambda)=1\).
statement: For a fixed integrable potential \(p\), the solution with initial data \((0,1)\) is entire in \(\lambda\), as are \(y(\pi,\lambda)\) and \(y'(\pi,\lambda)\). For fixed \((a,b)\ne(0,0)\), the separated right condition \(a y'(\pi)+b y(\pi)=0\) gives the characteristic function \(a y'(\pi,\lambda)+b y(\pi,\lambda)\). Its zeros are precisely the eigenvalues for the left Dirichlet condition. Initial data \((0,0)\) instead produce only the zero solution.
reconstruction: Integrability of the fixed potential and nonzero boundary coefficients are sufficient standard assumptions. The normalization repair is internal: the scan itself supplies \(y'(0,\lambda)=1\) below the erroneous margin.
fate: The differential-equation observation is classical and is independently checked by the Volterra integral equation; the cited Bott--Chern paper supplies the surrounding value-distribution theme, not this spectral argument. \citep{bottchern1965hermitian}
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: A value-distribution route to spectral completeness
notes: Gelfand asks how general considerations about an analytic curve in a function space could give completeness. A theorem for a Banach-space curve missing only finitely many hyperplanes is proposed with \ru{возм., неверно}.
statement: The notebook specifies neither a Banach space, a topology of completeness, nor a class of hyperplanes or curves sufficient to identify a spectral-completeness theorem. Moreover, a literal finite-omission assertion fails even for a linearly nondegenerate entire curve in \(\ell^2\): \[F(z)=(1,e^z,e^{2z}/2!,e^{3z}/3!,\ldots).\] Every coordinate is nonzero, so every coordinate hyperplane is omitted. If a continuous linear functional annihilates \(F\), the entire power series in \(w=e^z\) vanishes on \(\mathbb C^*\), so all its coefficients vanish.
reconstruction: \ours{} The displayed Hilbert-space counterexample and its linear nondegeneracy proof are this task's annotation of the broad proposed assertion. They do not purport to refute an unspecified stronger hypothesis that Gelfand might have intended.
fate: Bott--Chern does not state this Banach-space completeness theorem. Its finite-dimensional setting cannot be promoted to one. The notes themselves signal doubt; the intended spectral question remains insufficiently specified. \citep{bottchern1965hermitian}
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, the raw finite-omission proposal has the explicit counterexample above. A precise additional-hypothesis completeness problem has not been recovered, so this is F rather than an allegedly neglected open problem.

title: Distribution of simultaneous zeros in several complex variables
notes: The notes ask about the zeros of \(n\) functions in \(n\) variables and say that no satisfactory analogue of Nevanlinna theory exists.
statement: This is a research programme, not a single quantified conjecture: the source does not specify the domain, exhaustion, growth hypotheses, target geometry or defect inequality. Bott--Chern treats zero distribution of holomorphic sections in Hermitian bundles, providing a concrete portion of the programme. No theorem covering every possible meaning of satisfactory theory can be formulated from the sentence.
reconstruction: The exact subject of the named paper supplies context without supplying absent hypotheses.
fate: The explicitly cited 1965 paper already develops one version of the several-variable zero-distribution theory. Its scope does not turn this broad remark into a settled or unsettled universal conjecture. \citep{bottchern1965hermitian}
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, substantial several-variable value-distribution theories exist, but the notebook sentence has no precise residual question. No problem-index entry is assigned.

title: Bundle-valued forms and a connection
notes: \(A(X,E)=A(X)\otimes\Gamma(E)\), followed by a tensor-base entry read as \(A^0(E)\); the connection satisfies \(D(fs)=df\,s+fDs\).
statement: For a smooth finite-rank vector bundle \(E\to X\), \(A^\bullet(X,E)=\Omega^\bullet(X)\otimes_{C^\infty(X)}\Gamma(E)\). A connection is a real- or complex-linear map \(D:\Gamma(E)\to\Omega^1(X,E)\) with the displayed Leibniz rule. It extends to bundle-valued forms by \(D(\alpha\otimes s)=d\alpha\otimes s+(-1)^{\deg\alpha}\alpha\wedge Ds\).
reconstruction: The tensor base is \(A^0(X)=C^\infty(X)\), as the very next tensor formula in the notes confirms. The graded extension is made explicit because its sign controls subsequent curvature calculations.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Curvature in the notebook frame convention
notes: For \(Ds_i=\sum_j\theta_{ij}s_j\), the curvature is written \(K=d\theta-\theta\wedge\theta\). Matrix multiplication explains why \(\theta\wedge\theta\) need not vanish.
statement: Writing the frame as the column \(s=(s_i)\) with \(Ds=\theta s\) and extending \(D\) by the graded Leibniz rule gives \(D^2s=(d\theta-\theta\wedge\theta)s\). Thus \(K\) is a matrix of two-forms representing the curvature in this frame convention. The minus sign is consistent and should not be replaced by the plus sign used with another matrix convention.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Chern forms, normalization and cohomology classes
notes: The displayed determinant on P000112 has \(2\pi/i\), and the text calls the result closed two-forms; P000113 says that it is independent of the connection.
statement: For a complex vector bundle with connection, the total Chern form in the preceding convention is \[c(E,D)=\det\left(I+\frac{i}{2\pi}K\right)=1+c_1(E,D)+\cdots+c_r(E,D),\qquad c_j\in\Omega^{2j}(X).\] These forms are closed. Their de Rham cohomology classes are independent of the connection; their actual differential-form representatives generally vary with it.
reconstruction: The reciprocal coefficient on P000112 is a notebook mathematical error, not a transcription correction: the scan has it, whereas P000116 and P000119 give \(i/(2\pi)\). The distinction between a form and its class repairs the independence claim.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Change of frame and invariant determinant
notes: \(s'=As\) gives \(dA+A\theta=\theta'A\) and \(AK=K'A\). The intermediate differentiated line lacks a prime and has the wrong graded sign.
statement: For an invertible matrix \(A\) of smooth functions, \[\theta'=dA\,A^{-1}+A\theta A^{-1},\qquad K'=AKA^{-1}.\] Differentiating the first frame identity requires \(dA\wedge\theta+A\,d\theta=d\theta' A-\theta'\wedge dA\). Conjugacy of \(K\), together with commutativity of even scalar forms, makes \(\det(I+tK)\) independent of frame.

title: Left--right equivalence and structural stability of map germs
notes: The source studies \(f:M^m\to N^n\), or \((\mathbb R^m,0)\to(\mathbb R^n,0)\), up to changes of variables in source and target, and asks whether small perturbations remain equivalent.
statement: Two germs are smoothly left--right equivalent when \(g=k\circ f\circ h^{-1}\) for local diffeomorphisms \(h,k\). Local stability allows the singular point to move under perturbation. For a global map, stability means that an open neighbourhood in the Whitney smooth topology lies in its orbit under source and target diffeomorphisms. A topological variant replaces the equivalences by homeomorphisms.
reconstruction: Local stability with movable source/target points must be distinguished from equivalence of germs fixing the origin and from global stability.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Morse normal form and genericity
notes: For \(n=1\), nondegenerate \(d^2f\) gives a quadratic form, classified by index and signature; generic critical points are isolated, and the relevant set is open and dense for compact source.
statement: If \(df_p=0\) and the Hessian is nonsingular, smooth local coordinates give \(f=f(p)-x_1^2-\cdots-x_\lambda^2+x_{\lambda+1}^2+\cdots+x_m^2\). Morse functions form an open dense subset of \(C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)\) for compact \(M\). Global left--right stability additionally requires pairwise distinct critical values; nondegenerate critical points alone supply local stability.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Whitney fold and cusp normal forms for surface maps
notes: The three displayed models are regular, fold \((x_1^2,x_2)\), and cusp \((x_1,x_2^3-x_1x_2)\); the source attributes approximation by these types to Whitney (1955).
statement: A generic smooth map between surfaces has only regular points, folds and cusps; its critical set is a smooth curve, with isolated cusp points. The listed normal forms represent the local stable types. For global stability of a proper map, additional multisingularity conditions are needed: distinct fold branches meet transversely, only double fold intersections occur, and cusp images are separated from other critical images.
reconstruction: The global transversality conditions are not supplied by the list of local models. They are stated to prevent reading a local classification as a complete global criterion.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Cusp critical curve and its image
notes: For \((y_1,y_2)=(x_1,x_2^3-x_1x_2)\), the determinant is \(3x_2^2-x_1\). The source then writes \(y_2^2=-y_1^3\), \(y_1>0\), and initially calls the origin a fold.
statement: The critical curve is \((x_1,x_2)=(3t^2,t)\), mapped to \((y_1,y_2)=(3t^2,-2t^3)\). Thus \(27y_2^2=4y_1^3\). The origin is a cusp; every other nearby critical point is a fold. The family \(t\mapsto t^3-Ct\) is strictly increasing for \(C<0\), and has two critical points for \(C>0\), producing the familiar one-versus-three inverse-image regions.
reconstruction: \oursComputed{} The signs and coefficients follow directly by substitution, independently of publication identification. Both erroneous statements are visible in the scan; the later line correctly says that points away from zero are folds.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: The perturbation of a complex square by a conjugate-linear term
notes: The explicit exercise is \(z\mapsto z^2+\varepsilon\overline z\), with \(\varepsilon\ne0\), and the predicted singularities are folds and cusps.
statement: As a real map of the plane, \(F_\varepsilon\) has Jacobian \(4|z|^2-|\varepsilon|^2\). Its critical locus is the circle \(|z|=|\varepsilon|/2\). Rotations and positive rescalings reduce the caustic to \(w(t)=\tfrac14e^{2it}+\tfrac12e^{-it}\): its derivative vanishes exactly at \(e^{3it}=1\), giving three ordinary cusps and folds elsewhere. The critical image is a three-cusped hypocycloid.
reconstruction: \oursComputed{} The determinant, parameterization and cusp test are independently computed in this task. A nonzero complex \(\varepsilon\) is reduced to the same model by source/target rotations.
fate: Arnold's 1968 exposition, Example 6, printed pp. 4--5, gives exactly this perturbation and its three-cusp picture. No pre-November-1965 publication of this exact example was documented in this check; class A follows the verified later publication by the speaker, rather than inferring antiquity from its elementary character. \citep{arnold1968singularities}
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Rank strata and their expected codimension
notes: The notes discuss the independent minors of a rectangular rank-\(r\) matrix and call the corresponding \(\Sigma_r\) smooth submanifolds of the source.
statement: The rank-exactly-\(r\) locus in \(\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb R^m,\mathbb R^n)\) is smooth of codimension \((m-r)(n-r)\). For a map \(f\), its inverse image under the first jet is a smooth source submanifold of this codimension when the jet section is transverse to that matrix-rank stratum. Arbitrary maps need not have smooth rank loci.
reconstruction: The generic transversality condition separates a smooth universal jet stratum from its possibly singular inverse image.

title: Iterated coranks and the fold--cusp Boardman symbols

statement: With Boardman's convention, the first entry is \(\dim\ker df\), and successive entries are obtained by intrinsic derivative or Jacobian-ideal extensions. title: Boardman strata in jet space and generic transversality
notes: The notes name Boardman and replace the naive repeated-rank construction by a decomposition in spaces of truncated Taylor series.
statement: For every admissible finite Boardman symbol \(I\), the universal stratum \(\Sigma^I\) is a smooth locally closed submanifold of a sufficiently high jet space, with a universal codimension. title: Smooth, analytic and formal equivalence are different categories
notes: The record compares \(C^\infty\) germs, analytic germs and formal power series. Formal coordinate changes have invertible first derivative.
statement: A formal map germ fixing zero is invertible under formal composition exactly when its linear part is invertible. Analytic changes also require convergence; smooth changes may contain flat terms invisible to every finite jet and to the full Taylor series. Consequently equality or equivalence of Taylor series alone does not establish smooth or analytic equivalence without a finite-determinacy or convergence theorem.

title: Smooth moduli and the incompleteness of Boardman symbols
notes: The notes mention a \(\mathbb R^9\to\mathbb R^9\) example, infinitely many or continuous invariants in larger dimensions, and a smooth invariant that is not topological.
statement: Boardman symbols are coarse invariants and do not classify left--right orbits. title: Thom topological classification outside infinite codimension

statement: The identifiable historical formulation is a decomposition of germs into countably many finite-codimension pieces consisting of topologically equivalent germs, with an exceptional part of infinite jet-codimension. This is distinct from saying that every such germ is individually an open orbit. A related global theorem asserts density of topologically stable maps from a compact smooth manifold to any smooth manifold, in every dimension pair.

title: Infinitesimal stability and the source--target linearization
notes: For every variation \(\varphi\), the equation \(\varphi(x)=f'(x)h(x)+k(y)\) should be solvable; this is attributed to Mather, followed by the remark that the proof is incorrect.
statement: For a proper smooth map \(f:M\to N\), infinitesimal stability is the surjectivity of \[\Gamma(TM)\oplus\Gamma(TN)\longrightarrow\Gamma(f^*TN),\qquad(h,k)\longmapsto df(h)+k\circ f.\] In Mather's smooth theory it is equivalent to stability. Properness, the topology of maps, and the global or multigerm setting matter; an arbitrary Frechet-space inverse-function theorem does not prove the assertion.

fate: Mather's 1969 paper establishes the sufficient direction; Arnold's 1968 exposition reports the subsequently successful smooth proof and develops an analytic local argument. The 1965 criticism cannot be transferred to the final theorem. \citep{mather1969stability,arnold1968singularities}

title: The low-dimensional stability range and generic immersions
notes: The source lists \(\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2,\mathbb R^3\), calls the \(\mathbb R^4\) target case unknown, says \(\mathbb R^5\) has no singularities, and gives density through \(m=n=8\).

title: Bianchi identity and closed characteristic forms
notes: The displayed Bianchi identity is \(dK=-[K,\theta]\), described as the derivative of the curvature tensor.
statement: For \(K=d\theta-\theta\wedge\theta\), direct exterior differentiation gives \(dK=\theta\wedge K-K\wedge\theta=-[K,\theta]\). title: Connection variation and transgression

Consequently integrals over closed cycles are independent of the connection, but pointwise forms usually are not.

title: Natural metric tensors from curvature and its derivatives
notes: Gelfand asks how to find all tensors formed from \(g_{\alpha\beta}\) and its derivatives, then says they are algebraic expressions in curvature and its covariant derivatives.
statement: A finite-order natural tensor constructed from a Riemannian metric is determined in normal coordinates by the curvature tensor and finitely many covariant derivatives, equivariantly under changes of orthonormal frame. For polynomial natural tensors, invariant theory expresses them using tensor products, permutations and contractions with the metric and its inverse (and the volume tensor in an oriented setting). A general smooth natural invariant need only be a smooth function of such data; it need not be polynomial.

title: Relations among covariant derivatives of curvature

title: Normal-coordinate metric coefficients and their identities
notes: The source expands the metric without a linear term and says that all coefficients in a normal system are tensors; some Taylor indices are overwritten or repeated.
statement: In geodesic normal coordinates about \(p\), \(g_{ij}(0)\) is the prescribed inner product and \(\partial_k g_{ij}(0)=0\). Changing the frame at \(p\) changes normal coordinates linearly, so their higher coefficient arrays are tensors for that restricted frame-change action. In one standard curvature-sign convention, \(g_{ij}(x)=g_{ij}(0)-\tfrac13R_{ikjl}(p)x^kx^l+O(|x|^3)\). General coordinate partial derivatives of the metric are not tensors. The normal-coordinate identity \(g_x(x,v)=g_0(x,v)\) provides the coefficient constraints.

title: Structural stability of a flow and parameter-dependent families

title: Distinguished Weierstrass polynomials
notes: The notes write \(P(y)=y^n+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}y^ia_i(x,z)\), with \(a_i(0,0)=0\); the constant coefficient is absent.
statement: For parameter variables \(u=(x,z)\), a distinguished polynomial is \(P(y,u)=y^n+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_i(u)y^i\), where each \(a_i(0)=0\). The coefficients lie in the relevant analytic, formal or smooth germ ring. The term \(a_0\) is essential; omitting it forces divisibility by \(y\) and does not describe a general distinguished polynomial.

title: Analytic and formal Weierstrass division
notes: The stated division is \(f=PQ+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}b_i(u)y^i\), with coefficients and quotient of the same class; the quotient by \((P)\) is finite over the parameter ring.
statement: If \(P\) is a distinguished polynomial of degree \(n\), every analytic germ \(f(y,u)\) has a unique division \(f=PQ+R\), where \(Q\) is analytic and \(R=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}b_i(u)y^i\) has analytic coefficients. The analogous formal statement holds over characteristic-zero formal power-series rings. The analytic or formal quotient by \((P)\) is free of rank \(n\) over the parameter germ ring, with basis \(1,y,\ldots,y^{n-1}\). This is finite module rank, not finite dimension over the scalar field when parameters remain.

title: Smooth division and its loss of uniqueness
notes: Malgrange's \(C^\infty\) analogue is said to hold but without uniqueness.
statement: For a smooth distinguished polynomial near the origin and a smooth germ \(f\), smooth division produces a smooth quotient and a remainder polynomial in \(y\) of degree below \(n\), with smooth parameter coefficients. Such a representation need not be unique. The quotient module is finitely generated over the parameter ring; it must not automatically be called free of rank \(n\), because smooth flat terms can create relations.

title: Interpolation when the roots are real
notes: The notes propose Lagrange interpolation when the polynomial has \(n\) real roots, with a warning about smooth dependence.
statement: For distinct real roots, the remainder is determined by the values of \(f\) at the roots through Lagrange interpolation. At repeated real roots, Hermite interpolation prescribes derivatives to the corresponding multiplicities. Divided-difference formulae explain why the remainder has smooth symmetric dependence when roots coalesce; the naive formula with denominators of root differences requires this limiting argument. In the general non-real-root case smooth uniqueness fails.

title: The flat-function counterexample to unique division
notes: For a smooth function \(f(x)\) flat at zero, the notes divide by \(y^2+x^2\) in two ways and attribute smoothness of the nontrivial quotient to a Lojasiewicz argument.
statement: Let \(f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)\) satisfy \(f^{(j)}(0)=0\) for every \(j\). Put \(q(x,y)=f(x)/(x^2+y^2)\) off the origin and \(q(0,0)=0\). Then \(q\) is smooth and flat: every derivative is bounded by a finite sum of \(|f^{(j)}(x)|\,(x^2+y^2)^{-N}\), and flatness absorbs each denominator. Thus \(f=(x^2+y^2)\cdot0+f\) and \(f=(x^2+y^2)q+0\) are distinct smooth divisions when \(f\ne0\).

title: Preparation of a germ regular in one variable
notes: If \(f(0,0)=0\) and some \(\partial_y^n f(0,0)\ne0\), the notes write \(f=P Q\), with distinguished \(P\) and \(Q(0,0)\ne0\); nonflatness is said to allow this.

title: An essential circle meets its area-preserving image
notes: An area-preserving annulus diffeomorphism homotopic to the identity is said to satisfy \(\#(A\gamma\cap\gamma)\ge2\) for every closed curve surrounding the hole.
statement: Let \(A\) be an area-preserving diffeomorphism of a compact annulus, isotopic to the identity, and let \(\gamma\) be an embedded essential circle in its interior. If \(A\gamma\) and \(\gamma\) meet transversely, they have at least two intersections. Were they disjoint, one would lie strictly on one side of the other and the enclosed annular region would contradict equality of the area between each curve and the same boundary component. A transverse intersection count between isotopic essential circles is even.

title: Globally canonical transformations and exactness
notes: On \(T^n\times B^n\), the notes impose \(\oint_{A\gamma}p\,dq=\oint_\gamma p\,dq\) for closed loops, calling this globally canonical.
statement: With \(\lambda=\sum p_i\,dq_i\), equality of these integrals for every closed loop is equivalent to \(A^*\lambda-\lambda=dS\) for a global smooth function \(S\), assuming a connected domain. Differentiating gives \(A^*d\lambda=d\lambda\), so \(A\) is exact symplectic. Ordinary symplecticity only makes the difference closed. A compactly supported Hamiltonian isotopy has exact time-one map; an exact endpoint homotopic to the identity should not be silently substituted for a specified Hamiltonian isotopy without an additional argument.

title: Arnold torus-intersection bound and the missing transversality
notes: For the zero torus \(T=\{p=0\}\), the notebook labels \(\#(AT\cap T)\ge2^n\) a theorem, but proves only the graphical case under an additional assumption. No transversality is written.
statement: A precise established version is: if \(\phi\) is a compactly supported Hamiltonian diffeomorphism of \(T^*T^n\) and \(\phi(T^n)\) meets the zero section transversely, then \(\#(\phi(T^n)\cap T^n)\ge\sum_j b_j(T^n;\mathbb F_2)=2^n\). Without transversality the universal cup-length lower bound is \(n+1\). The literal \(2^n\) assertion is false already for \(n=2\): \(S(x,y)=\sin x+\sin y-\sin(x+y)\) has exactly three critical points, and a small graph of \(dS\) is a Hamiltonian image of the zero section.

fate: Chaperon's 1983 exposition records the torus progress; the transverse Floer bound and the cotangent-bundle nontransverse cup-length theorem are checked in the opened later sources. title: The graph argument reduces intersections to Morse critical points
notes: The notes assume \(AT\) can be written \(p=p(q)\) and finish by invoking Morse theory on the torus.

Its intersections with the zero section are exactly \(\operatorname{Crit}(S)\), and they are transverse precisely when \(S\) is Morse. Morse inequalities imply at least \(2^n\) such points. For a general smooth \(S\), Lusternik--Schnirelmann cup length gives at least \(n+1\) distinct critical points; it does not imply \(2^n\).

title: Type decomposition on a holomorphic bundle
notes: \(d=d'+d''\), \(D=D'+D''\), with bidegrees \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\); the notes call these two connections.
statement: On a complex manifold, \(d=\partial+\bar\partial\) and \(\Omega^k=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}\Omega^{p,q}\). Any complex connection splits into operators \(D'\) and \(D''\) of the corresponding bidegrees. They are partial connections, with Leibniz terms \(\partial f\) and \(\bar\partial f\), rather than two separate full connections. The local generators of scalar \((p,q)\)-forms use holomorphic coordinate functions and their conjugates; the \(f_i\) in that display are not sections of an arbitrary vector bundle.
reconstruction: The word connection in the split display is interpreted as partial connection. The reference to analytic sections in the form generators is repaired to local holomorphic scalar coordinates.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Existence and uniqueness of the Chern connection
notes: The headline says that a Hermitian metric determines a unique compatible connection; the numbered conditions additionally require \(D''s=0\) for holomorphic \(s\).
statement: On a holomorphic vector bundle \(E\) with a smooth positive-definite Hermitian metric \(h\), there is a unique connection preserving \(h\) and satisfying \(D''=\bar\partial_E\). The metric alone allows many compatible connections; compatibility with the specified holomorphic structure supplies the uniqueness condition. A local holomorphic frame then has connection matrix of type \((1,0)\).
reconstruction: The two numbered conditions, read together, recover the correct theorem despite the abbreviated headline.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Hermitian pairing of bundle-valued forms
notes: The displayed formula is \(\langle s\otimes\alpha,s'\otimes\beta\rangle=\langle s,s'\rangle\alpha\wedge\beta\), with no visible conjugation over \(\beta\).
statement: With the Hermitian metric linear in its first argument, the natural sesquilinear form-valued pairing is \(h(s\otimes\alpha,s'\otimes\beta)=h(s,s')\alpha\wedge\overline\beta\). The conjugation is required for compatibility with moving a complex scalar between the section and form factors. For homogeneous bundle-valued forms, the differential compatibility formula has the usual graded sign.

title: The metric matrix determines the Chern connection matrix
notes: \(N_{ij}=\langle s_i,s_j\rangle\), \(dN=\theta N+N\overline\theta^t\), hence \(d'N=\theta N\) and \(\theta=d'N\,N^{-1}\).
statement: For a local holomorphic row frame and a metric linear in the first argument, \(N\) is a positive Hermitian matrix. Metric compatibility gives \(dN=\theta N+N\overline\theta^t\), and the \((1,0)\)-part yields the uniquely determined matrix \(\theta=(\partial N)N^{-1}\). This matrix has the connection transformation law under holomorphic frame changes.

title: The Maurer--Cartan identity and the mistaken minus sign
notes: The notes first write \(d'\theta=\theta\wedge\theta\), then question it, and differentiate \(\theta=d'N\,N^{-1}\) with a minus sign on the resulting product.
statement: The positive identity is correct: \[\partial\theta=-\partial N\wedge\partial(N^{-1})=(\partial N)N^{-1}\wedge(\partial N)N^{-1}=\theta\wedge\theta.\] Both the graded Leibniz sign from the one-form \(\partial N\) and the sign in \(\partial N^{-1}=-N^{-1}(\partial N)N^{-1}\) are needed; they cancel.
reconstruction: \ours{} This graded calculation identifies exactly the missing sign. The minus in the handwritten differentiated line is genuine, so it is retained in the source apparatus.

title: Curvature of type (1,1), Bianchi, and Chern-form types
notes: \(K=d''\theta\), \(d''K=0\), \(d'K=-[K,\theta]\); the notes conclude that all characteristic classes have type \((p,p)\).
statement: For the Chern connection, \(K=\bar\partial\theta\) has type \((1,1)\), \(\bar\partial K=0\), and \(\partial K=-[K,\theta]\), where the bracket is the graded matrix commutator. Consequently \(c_j(E,h)\) has type \((j,j)\), is closed, and represents the de Rham Chern class. On a general non-Kahler manifold this statement concerns a representative; it does not presume a Hodge decomposition of all de Rham cohomology.

title: Curvature of a Hermitian holomorphic line bundle
notes: In rank one, \(N(x)>0\), \(\theta=d'\log N\) and \(K=d''d'\log N\); the characteristic class is the same up to a factor.
statement: In a local nonvanishing holomorphic section \(s\), put \(N=h(s,s)\). Then \(K=\bar\partial\partial\log N\), and \(c_1(E,h)=\frac{i}{2\pi}\bar\partial\partial\log N\). Under holomorphic rescaling of \(s\), the extra logarithm is pluriharmonic, so the curvature glues globally. The order \(\bar\partial\partial\) matches the notebook's row-frame convention.

title: Watts tensor complex and its differential
notes: \(F^0=\Lambda\), \(F^p=\Lambda\otimes_KF^{p-1}\), insertion maps \(d_i\) add a unit, and \(d^p=\sum(-1)^id_i\). The prose calls \(F^p\) functions of \(p\) variables.
statement: For a commutative unital \(K\)-algebra \(\Lambda\), set \(F^p=\Lambda^{\otimes_K(p+1)}\). For \(0\le i\le p+1\), let \(d_i:F^p\to F^{p+1}\) insert \(1\) in position \(i\), and put \(d^p=\sum_{i=0}^{p+1}(-1)^id_i\). The cosimplicial insertion identities imply \(d^{p+1}d^p=0\). For a function algebra, a simple tensor is a function of \(p+1\) variables, not \(p\); no completion to all continuous functions on the product is part of this algebraic definition.

title: Algebraic germs along the diagonal
notes: \(\mu(f_0\otimes\cdots\otimes f_p)=f_0\cdots f_p\); for a maximal ideal \(M\subset\Lambda\), an element vanishes near \(M\) if it dies upon localization at \(\mu^{-1}M\).
statement: The multiplication map \(\mu_p:F^p\to\Lambda\) is a surjective algebra homomorphism, so \(\mu_p^{-1}M\) is maximal. An element \(f\in F^p\) maps to zero in \((F^p)_{\mu_p^{-1}M}\) exactly if there exists \(g\notin\mu_p^{-1}M\) with \(gf=0\). For \(\Lambda=C(X,\mathbb R)\) and compact Hausdorff \(X\), maximal ideals correspond to points and \(\mu\) is restriction to the diagonal.

title: The quotient by functions locally zero at the diagonal
notes: \(N^p\) consists of elements vanishing in a strip around the diagonal; \(d^pN^p\subset N^{p+1}\), and the notes call the resulting \(H^p\) homology.
statement: Let \(N^p=\bigcap_{M\in\operatorname{Max}\Lambda}\ker(F^p\to(F^p)_{\mu_p^{-1}M})\). The insertion differential preserves this family, so \(F^\bullet/N^\bullet\) is a cochain complex. Its degree-\(p\) group is cohomology, \(H^p=\ker d^p/\operatorname{im}d^{p-1}\). For a compact function space, the local condition is vanishing on some neighborhood of the whole diagonal.

title: Recovering Alexander--Spanier cohomology from C(X)
notes: The final parenthesis says that the groups agree with ordinary Alexander--Spanier cohomology; Watts, PNAS 54(4), October 1965, is named.
statement: For compact Hausdorff \(X\), the preceding construction with \(K=\mathbb R\) and \(\Lambda=C(X,\mathbb R)\) computes Alexander--Spanier cohomology \(H^p(X;\mathbb R)\). Thus this cohomology is determined functorially by the unital real algebra of continuous real functions. The statement does not identify the construction for every abstract algebra with the cohomology of an unspecified spectrum.
fate: The exact two-page source was published in PNAS 54(4), 1027--1028, in October 1965 and is read in full. The talk is reporting that result, not posing a new cohomology problem. \citep{watts1965alexander}

notes: The notes cite Duke 1961, pp. 345--353, and assume finite order \(n\) in \(y\). An analytic coordinate change makes \(f\) a polynomial in the new \(y\), with analytic coefficients in the other variables.

Let \(f(y,x)\) be an analytic germ with \(\partial_y^j f(0,0)=0\) for \(j<n\) and \(\partial_y^n f(0,0)
e0\). There are an analytic local coordinate \(u=u(y,x)\), with \(\partial_yu(0,0)

e0\) and \(a_j(0)=0\) for \(j<n\). This is polynomialization after a coordinate change, not merely Weierstrass preparation with an extra unit factor.

title: Polynomialization of analytic functions of two variables
notes: The next line says that with two variables one can make an actual polynomial, without further qualifications.
statement: A safe precise version is that an analytic function germ with an isolated critical point is analytically right-equivalent to a polynomial germ, by finite determinacy; this includes the corresponding two-variable case. The precise maximum generality of Levinson's cited two-variable formulation has not been checked in its original full text here. The unrestricted wording in this line is not used to infer that every analytic germ in any dimension is polynomializable, or to identify a new unresolved classification problem.

title: Whitney example with five branches
notes: The example is \(xy(y-x)(y-xz)(x\varphi(z)-y)\), with \(\varphi(0)=0\) and \(\varphi\) transcendental; the notes say four surfaces but later use the two quadruples \((1,2,3,4)\) and \((1,2,3,5)\).
statement: Choose an analytic germ \(\varphi\) algebraically transcendental over \(\mathbb C(z)\), for example \(e^z-1\). The five factors define five smooth surface germs meeting along the \(z\)-axis, with generically distinct tangent planes away from exceptional axis points. This is the Whitney-type construction of an analytic three-variable germ whose zero-set geometry obstructs polynomialization by a smooth local diffeomorphism. Its critical locus is nonisolated, so it does not contradict finite determinacy at isolated critical points.
reconstruction: \ours{} Five, rather than four, branches are forced by the product and by the two listed quadruples. Algebraic transcendence, rather than merely being a nonpolynomial analytic function, is the property needed by the cross-ratio argument.
fate: Arnold's 1968 exposition, printed p. 39, reproduces Whitney's five-factor counterexample with an exponential factor and attributes it to Whitney's 1965 work. The notebook's parameterized variant has the same mechanism, but its overwritten factors prevent a letter-for-letter exact match. \citep{arnold1968singularities}

title: The pair of cross-ratios obstructs algebraic realization
notes: The anharmonic ratio of tangent planes through a common line is called a diffeomorphism invariant. A curve in the two cross-ratio coordinates is transcendental for the example but would be algebraic for a polynomial.
statement: Modulo the common tangent line, five tangent planes give five points of a projective line. A local diffeomorphism acts by one projective linear transformation on this normal plane, hence preserves the two cross-ratios formed using the first three marked planes. After fixed rational changes of cross-ratio coordinates, the resulting parameterized curve is \(z\mapsto(z,\varphi(z))\). A polynomial configuration yields an algebraic cross-ratio relation along its algebraic multiple-branch locus; choosing \(\varphi\) algebraically transcendental contradicts that relation. Permuting the finitely many branches only applies finitely many rational coordinate changes and does not remove the obstruction.
reconstruction: The argument is local on the open axis stratum with distinct planes; it does not assume that the coordinate change itself is analytic. The five-branch count and algebraic-transcendence requirement make the sketch precise.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: Arnold analytic decomposition of a stationary flow
notes: For an analytic stationary velocity in a bounded domain, not everywhere collinear with its curl, finitely many analytic pieces separate cells with torus windings or cylindrical rotations.
statement: Let \(D\) be a connected compact three-dimensional real-analytic Riemannian domain with real-analytic boundary, and let \(v\) be a real-analytic stationary incompressible Euler field tangent to the boundary, analytic up to it. Assume \(v\times\operatorname{curl}v\) is not identically zero. Outside a proper compact analytic exceptional set, regular Bernoulli level components are embedded tori or annuli. On a torus the streamlines are conjugate to a constant linear flow and hence are closed or dense; on an annulus they are closed. The critical values of the Bernoulli function, including its boundary restriction, determine finitely many regular cells.
reconstruction: Compactness, analyticity through the boundary, the global Bernoulli function, and the exceptional critical-level set are explicit. Boundedness and interior analyticity alone do not give the stated finiteness.
fate: Theorem 7 in Arnold's full 1966 paper, printed pp. 346--348, is an exact expanded match and cites his 1965 C. R. Acad. Sci. note, volume 261, p. 17. The result was therefore already announced before this December talk. \citep{arnold1966geometrie}

title: A common first integral for two commuting divergence-free fields
notes: The compact-orbit proof writes \(\operatorname{rot}(a\ast b)=0\), then calls \(a\times b\) a differential and identifies orbits with level surfaces.
statement: On an oriented volume three-manifold \((M,\mu)\), if \(a,b\) preserve \(\mu\) and commute, the one-form \(\alpha=\iota_b\iota_a\mu\) is closed. If \(H^1(M;\mathbb R)=0\), then \(\alpha=dF\). Both fields are tangent to the levels of \(F\). Where they are independent, \(dF\ne0\), and their joint orbit is open in the connected regular level component. This last step does not identify a singular-level orbit with an entire closed level set.
reconstruction: \ours{} Cartan's identity gives \(d\alpha=\mathcal L_b\iota_a\mu-\iota_b\mathcal L_a\mu=0\). Regularity and rank two are the missing steps in the notebook's orbit-to-level inference.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: A compact regular joint orbit is a torus
notes: The notes say that compact orbits without boundary are tori, with the one-parameter velocity action giving a winding.
statement: Let \(C\) be a compact connected regular level surface without boundary on which the two commuting fields \(a,b\) are everywhere independent and tangent. Their complete flows define a locally free \(\mathbb R^2\)-action. Every orbit is open; connectedness makes the action transitive, so \(C\simeq\mathbb R^2/\Lambda\) for a discrete cocompact subgroup \(\Lambda\), necessarily a rank-two lattice. Thus \(C\simeq T^2\), and either field is a constant linear flow in these action coordinates. Its individual streamline may be dense and nonclosed although the joint \(\mathbb R^2\)-orbit is compact.
reconstruction: \ours{} The action-and-lattice argument supplies the rank and completeness qualifications. Compact joint orbits are not confused with compact or closed individual streamlines.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: The assertion that every joint orbit is compact is false
notes: The separately labelled mathematical theorem assumes \(b_1=0\), a finite or compact manifold, and two commuting divergence-free fields, and concludes that their orbits are compact.
statement: These hypotheses do not force compact joint orbits. On the round \(S^3\subset\mathbb C^2\), let \(a(z_1,z_2)=(iz_1,i\alpha z_2)\), with \(\alpha\notin\mathbb Q\), and let \(b=0\). Both fields are smooth, complete and divergence-free, they commute, and \(H^1(S^3;\mathbb R)=0\). Through a point with \(z_1z_2\ne0\), the joint \(\mathbb R^2\)-orbit equals the irrational \(a\)-orbit and is dense but nonclosed in a Clifford torus, hence noncompact. The common first integral here is constant; its level set is not the orbit.
reconstruction: \ours{} The explicit counterexample isolates the missing rank/regular-level hypothesis. The term joint orbit is used deliberately: the failure is in the asserted \(\mathbb R^2\)-orbit theorem itself.
fate: Arnold's published proof only uses compact regular Bernoulli components with two independent tangent fields, as in item 1965-76.6; it does not state this unrestricted compact-orbit lemma. \citep{arnold1966geometrie}
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, the literal standalone assertion is disproved by the displayed example; the regular-level torus theorem is established. No open compact-orbit problem is extracted.

title: Boundary components give annuli with closed streamlines
notes: The notes say that noncompact orbits are cylinders and illustrate fluid between rotating coaxial cylinders, with neighboring rings turning in opposite directions.
statement: For a compact regular Bernoulli level component \(C\) meeting the boundary transversely in Arnold's setting, each boundary component is a closed velocity orbit. Commutation and independence propagate its period through \(C\), and \(C\) is an annulus with closed streamlines. It is not a theorem that every noncompact two-dimensional orbit of an \(\mathbb R^2\)-action is a cylinder: a trivial stabilizer gives a plane, while a rank-one stabilizer gives a cylinder. The rotating-cylinder sketch is a qualitative illustration and does not by itself establish an inviscid or viscous Taylor--Couette instability theorem.
reconstruction: The boundary annulus is distinguished from a general noncompact homogeneous orbit. No viscosity, rotation rate, onset threshold or boundary-value problem is recoverable from the sketch.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this is an established result in the stated setting; the notebook occurrence does not leave a separate open problem.

title: The everywhere-collinear or Beltrami exception
notes: If velocity and vorticity are everywhere collinear, the notebook asserts that examples need not have the stated simple orbit structure, without giving an explicit example.
statement: If \(v\times\omega\equiv0\), the Bernoulli function is constant on a connected domain, and the nonconstant-first-integral proof of the torus/annulus structure is unavailable. The notebook does not identify a particular Beltrami field or a specific dynamical obstruction. Arnold's 1966 discussion lists the trigonometric ABC-type field as an example of this exceptional class, but describes complicated streamline topology there as probable, not as proved in that paper.
fate: The exceptional case is explicitly discussed in Arnold's paper, printed p. 347 and its footnote. The particular counterexample claimed orally is not identifiable from the notebook, and the paper's speculative language is not upgraded to a proof. \citep{arnold1966geometrie}
present_status: As of 9 November 2026, this occurrence identifies the limitation of the regular Bernoulli-level theorem but not a precise open problem or a verified historical example. No general Beltrami-flow conjecture is imported.

title: Yudovich global two-dimensional existence and uniqueness
notes: The notes mention short-time existence and, in two dimensions, existence and uniqueness, with the explicit parenthesis Yudovich.
statement: A precise unforced specialization is: on a bounded simply connected planar domain with \(C^2\) boundary, an initial divergence-free velocity tangent to the boundary with bounded vorticity determines a unique global Euler solution in the class of velocities with bounded vorticity. Smooth initial data yield the corresponding classical solution. The historical local classical three-dimensional result and the two-dimensional global bounded-vorticity result are different theorems; the Yudovich citation concerns inviscid Euler, not an assertion that viscosity is present.

title: Hamiltonian spectral symmetry in the inviscid limit
notes: At \(\nu=0\) the spectrum is said to be symmetric about both axes, with a partly unclear Hamiltonian parenthesis.
statement: For a real finite-dimensional Hamiltonian linearization \(A=JH\), where \(J\) is invertible skew-symmetric and \(H\) symmetric, eigenvalues occur with their algebraic multiplicities in the set \(\lambda,-\lambda,\overline\lambda,-\overline\lambda\). Reality gives conjugation and the Hamiltonian identity gives sign symmetry. title: Inertia operator and the left-invariant Riemannian metric
notes: \(L:\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak g^*\) is symmetric positive definite and \(\langle a,b\rangle_g=\langle dL_{g^{-1}}a,dL_{g^{-1}}b\rangle_e\).

title: Free rigid-body motion as a geodesic on SO(3)
notes: For \(G=SO(3)\), geodesics describe rotation of a rigid body about a fixed point; the metric is kinetic energy.
statement: For a rigid body with a fixed point and no applied torque, the positive inertia tensor defines a left-invariant kinetic-energy metric on \(SO(3)\). Its geodesics are precisely the free rotations, with the usual factor \(1/2\) in kinetic energy. An asymmetric top generally has a left-invariant metric that is not bi-invariant; no external potential or torque is included.

title: Euler flow as a geodesic of the right-invariant L2 metric

title: The affine group realizes the hyperbolic plane

title: Left and right trivializations of tangent and cotangent vectors
